# Fitting models

The goal is to assign each 48×48 face to one of four emotions: anger, disgust, happiness or sadness. 
We evaluate models by **classification accuracy**, the share of images classified correctly. As mentioned in the introduction of the notebook, 
humans reach about **74.4%** accuracy on this task, so we expect to do better than that with machine learning using the features
we've built in section 3. 
 
We compare three statistcial models, ordered from least to most flexible:

1. **Lasso multinomial logistic regression**
2. **Random forest**: 
3. **Support vector machine with a radial kernel**

Looking at both less and more flexible models allows us to see how the bias–variance trade-off plays out in practice. A less flexible method has 
higher bias (it cannot follow the true class boundaries closely) but lower variance (it is less sensitive to the particular training images).
 Which effect dominates depends on the data, so we cannot tell in
advance which method will have the highest test accuracy. Instead, we estimate it.

**How we measure performance.** We estimate test accuracy with 5-fold
cross-validation, with the folds grouped by subject. We do this because the file names
start with a subject ID (`S005`, `S010`, ...), and `caret::groupKFold()` puts all images
of one person in the same fold. Each held-out fold therefore contains only people the model has not seen during training. 
This matters because the training set contains augmented copies of images and
neighbouring frames from the same video, which are nearly identical. With random
folds, duplicates (in different rotationes) of the same face would end up in both the training and the
validation folds. The model can then score well by recognising the person rather than
the expression, and the cross-validation estimate of the test accuracy might be too
optimistic. Since all three models are evaluated on the same cross-validation folds, 
differences in model accuracy is not due to different splits of the data, but rather to the models themselves.

All models are trained on the built features from Section 3 (feature-construction), not on the 2,304 raw pixels.
The features summarize shapes, edges and brightness in the facial regions that differ between expressions.

```{r classification-functions, code=readLines("R/evaluation/classification.R"), fold="Classification evaluation function", message=FALSE}
source("R/evaluation/classification.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r resampling-settings}
set.seed(2023)
subjects <- sub("_.*", "", basename(rownames(x_train)))
folds <- caret::groupKFold(subjects, k = 5)
control <- caret::trainControl("cv", 5, index = folds, allowParallel = TRUE)
models <- list()
```

## Lasso multinomial logistic regression

The first model is multinomial logistic regression with an lasso
penalty on the coefficients. It models the log-odds between each pair of
emotions as a linear function of the features. We start with the lasso model because we 
have many engineered features compared with the number of
subjects, so an unpenalized model would have high variance. The lasso penalty shrinks
the coefficients towards zero and sets some of them to exactly zero. This both selects a
smaller set of features and reduces variance. Because its decision boundaries are linear
in the features, it is the least flexible of our three models and serves as a baseline.

The penalty strength λ controls the flexibility of the model. A larger λ sets more
coefficients to zero, which lowers variance but raises bias. With λ = 0 we get ordinary
multinomial logistic regression.  We choose our λ by cross-validation, where we try a grid 
of 20 values from 1 down to 0.0001 and pick the one with the highest accuracy.
We use this best λ rather than the one-standard-error rule, because our goal is prediction accuracy rather than the simplest model.

The features are standardized before fitting, so that each has standard deviation one.
A feature measured on a large scale needs only a small coefficient, so it would be
penalized less than a feature measured on a small scale. Standardizing puts all
features on an equal footing. The `glmnet()` function we're using does this by default.

```{r lasso-function, code=readLines("R/models/lasso.R"), fold="Lasso function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/lasso.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-lasso}
set.seed(2023)
models$lasso <- fit_lasso(features_train, y, control)
lasso <- models$lasso

lasso$bestTune # which lambda was chosen by cross-validation
lasso$results # Accuracy and Accuracy SD for chosen lambda
caret::confusionMatrix(lasso) # which emotions get confused, and Accuracy per class
```

Cross-validation selected λ = [LAMBDA]. The model reached a cross-validated accuracy of
90.3% (SD across folds: [CV_SD] percentage points), which is above the human
benchmark of 74.4%. Most errors came from confusing sad with anger, while
happy was recognised best (98.5% correct).

The lasso's decision boundaries are linear and additive in the features, so it cannot
capture interactions such as "brows lowered and mouth closed". Such a combination could
be a strong indicator of anger, but the lasso can only use it if we add it as a new
feature. Tree-based methods pick up interactions and non-linear effects automatically,
so we next fitted a random forest to test whether this flexibility improves classification accuracy.

## Random forest
A single classification tree would be the simplest tree-based option, but it has high
variance. A small change in the training data can produce a very different tree, and
single trees are usually less accurate than other methods. A random
forest addresses this. It grows many trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training
images, and classifies an image by majority vote, and thus averaging many trees reduces the
variance. In addition, at each split a tree may only choose from a fresh random subset of m of
the p features, which ends up decorrelating the trees. Without it, most trees would split on the
same few strong features first and look very similar, and averaging similar trees
reduces the variance much less. This suits our features well. Many of them are strongly correlated, 
for example the HOG features of the same region computed on 2×2 and 4×4 grids. 

The number of features per split (m), controls how different the trees are.
We consider m = √p features at each split, the standard choice for random forests models,
which makes the trees clearly different from each other while still giving each split
enough features to choose a good one. In a random forest, adding more trees (B) does not lead to overfitting. 
More trees only make the predictions more stable, so B just needs to be large enough for the error to
stop changing. Thus we choose to use B = 300.
Furthermore, we choose to stop splitting a node once it contains 10 or fewer images.
This is because it keeps the individual trees somewhat shallower and less flexible, while the
averaging over trees keeps the variance under control.

```{r forest-function, code=readLines("R/models/random_forest.R"), fold="Random forest function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/random_forest.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-forest}
set.seed(2023)
models$forest <- fit_random_forest(features_train, y, control)
forest <- models$forest

forest$results # m, Accuracy and , Accuracy SD
caret::confusionMatrix(forest) # which emotions get confused, and Accuracy per class
```

Contrary to what we expectated, the random forest performed worse than the lasso, with a
cross-validated accuracy of 82.3% (SD across folds: 8.2 percentage points) compared with
90.3% for the lasso. The drop came mainly from sad faces. The forest-model recognised only about
31% of them, and misclassifyed most of them as anger. This might suggest that 
for our features, the gain from modelling interactions between them did not outweigh the
cost of the forest model's weaker handling of the smaller, harder-to-distinguish classes (such as sadness and anger).

A random forest makes its decisions by asking simple yes/no questions about one feature at
a time, so the borders it draws between emotions are made up of small (kind of blocky) steps. This
works poorly when the difference between two emotions depends on several features
together, which may explain why the forest still often confused sad faces with anger and
disgust (seen in the confusion matrix above). A support vector machine with a radial kernel is a natural next step, 
since it can draw one smooth, curved border that takes all features into account at once. Thus it
combines the strength of the lasso, which also uses all features at once, with
the ability to capture interactions and non-linear effects that the lasso cannot.

## Radial SVM
Instead of a support vector classifier with a linear boundary, we use a SVM with a radial kernel.
The loss function of the linear support vector classifier is very similar to that of logistic regression, 
so the two often give very similar results, and our lasso model already covers a linear boundary. 
Like the support vector classifier, the radial SVM looks for a boundary with a wide margin between the
classes, while allowing some images to fall on the wrong side of the margin. However, the radial
kernel makes the boundary non-linear. Adittionally, it is local, meaning that an image is classified
mainly by the training images close to it in the feature space, while distant images play
almost no role. Because we have four emotions, we use a one-versus-one
approach. This way we fit a separate SVM for each of the six pairs of emotions and assigns each
image to the emotion that wins the most of these pairwise comparisons.

The radial SVM has two settings. `cost` sets how strongly the model is penalised when
images fall on the wrong side of the margin. A higher cost gives a narrower margin and a
more flexible boundary, which fits the training data more closely but is more likely to
overfit. We use cost = 4. `γ` sets how far each training image's influence reaches. With a larger γ, 
only very close images affect a prediction, so the boundary becomes more wiggly and more likely to overfit.
Because distances between images grow as more features are added, we scale γ by the number
of features p and use γ = 0.1/p.

Before fitting, we remove features that never vary and standardise the rest, and do this separately
within each training fold. As with the lasso, this matters because the radial kernel
relies on distances between images, so features measured on a larger scale would
otherwise dominate.

```{r svm-function, code=readLines("R/models/radial_svm.R"), fold="Radial SVM function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/radial_svm.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r fit-svm}
set.seed(2023)
models$svm_radial <- fit_radial_svm(features_train, y, control)
radial_svm <- models$svm_radial
radial_svm$results # CV accuracy and its SD
caret::confusionMatrix(radial_svm) # which emotions get confused
```

The radial SVM was the best of the three models, with a cross-validated accuracy of 92.3%
(SD across folds: 3.5 percentage points). This is above both the lasso (90.3%) and the
random forest (82.3%), and well above the human benchmark of 74.4%. Happy faces were
recognised almost perfectly (99.7% correct), followed by disgust (95.2%) and anger (89.8%).
Sad faces remained the most difficult to classify (71.4% correct). As with the other models, most
of these errors came from sad faces being classified as anger, which happened to about 25% of them.

## Comparing the models
Because all three models were evaluated on the same subject-grouped folds, we can
compare their cross-validated accuracies directly. The table below lists each model's
mean accuracy over the five folds and its training time, sorted from best to worst.

```{r compare-models}
# Compare models on the same folds
resampling <- caret::resamples(models)
model_comparison <- summary(resampling)$statistics$Accuracy |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  select(model, accuracy = Mean) |>
  mutate(seconds = sapply(models[model], function(m) m$times$everything[["elapsed"]])) |>
  arrange(dplyr::desc(accuracy))
model_comparison
```

As always, it's useful to check how well the algorithm performs on the training set: If
it doesn't classify the training set accurately, how can you expect better results on
the test set? This seemingly obvious point is often overlooked—surprisingly.

```{r evaluate-models}
cat("Evaluating models on training set...\n")
training_performance <- lapply(models, function(model) {
  predictions <- predict(model, features_train, type = "raw")
  evaluate_classification(predictions, y)
})
training_performance
```

On the training set, the lasso and the random forest classified 100% of the images
correctly and the radial SVM 99.9%, compared with their cross-validated accuracies of 90.3%,
82.3% and 92.3%. None of the models underfits badly. The gap between training and
cross-validated accuracy is 9.7 percentage points for the lasso, 17.7 for the forest and
7.6 for the SVM. Unlike what the bias–variance trade-off would suggest, the gap doesn't just grow with flexibility. 
For example, the SVM which is a more flexible model than the lasso, has the
smallest gap. This might be because we have more features than images (about 3,145
features for 2,538 images). Hence, even the linear lasso can fit the training images
perfectly. In this case, how well a model generalises depends less on how flexible its
boundary is and more on how well it avoids fitting noise. For the forest, a high training
accuracy is expected, since its trees are grown deep. We therefore choose between
the models by their cross-validated accuracy, not their training accuracy (Section 5).
